title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
description: Figure caption, Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU?ByKatya AdlerEurope editorIs Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot
body: Figure caption, Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU?ByKatya AdlerEurope editorIs Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else."We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians. Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU. But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs. They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.Figure caption, Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with EuropeCanada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

schema.headline: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees

title: Man City 5-0 Norwich: Floyd Samba debut overshadows JJ Gabriel saga
description: Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from anoth
body: Floyd Samba's scintillating first-team debut not only stole the show at Etihad Stadium on Thursday but also snatched all the headlines away from another high-profile teenager in Manchester.Website articles, social media posts and column inches have been filled this week with the news that highly rated 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel is on the verge of leaving Manchester United.But that particular saga will be overshadowed in Friday's football cuttings by 17-year-old Samba's stunning bow on the professional stage, scoring twice in Manchester City's 5-0 Carabao Cup third-round thrashing of Norwich City.Samba was prolific in City's under-18 side last season and those impressive performances led to him being promoted to the first-team set-up by new manager Enzo Maresca this summer.The show of faith is already being repaid."I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team," Samba told BBC Radio 5 Live. "To get a debut like that is mind-blowing."I couldn't believe it myself - but that is just the beginning, I have got a big career ahead of me. It was a great debut."I spoke to all of them [first-team players], they have all been brilliant with me - before the game, giving me advice like 'play your game, be you' - those words have given me confidence and helped me score those two goals today."The youngster joined City's academy at under-nine level and he really started to make a name for himself last term.Samba scored 24 goals and provided 10 assists in an eye-catching first full season with the under-18s, including curling home a stunning free-kick to help City win the FA Youth Cup final against rivals Manchester United in May.On his debut, Samba played the entire 90 minutes and fully grasped his opportunity.With City struggling for openings, Samba broke the deadlock by flicking home a header - he celebrated by blowing a kiss in the direction of family and friends in the stands, before curling in a delightful second later in the game.Samba was afforded a generous ovation towards the end of the game when being deservedly named man of the match."[I'm] satisfied not just for the goals but for the performance too," said manager Maresca."I asked him in the last three, four days - when I decided to play him as nine - he said he never played there. He is not a nine for sure, but he was good."He is young, full of energy, strong, can finish, can set [players up]. He made some good decisions in the first half. I am happy but they are young and we have to go slowly, slowly."Hopefully we can give him more chances."The Samba surname will be familiar to those of a certain age who have followed the Premier League.Floyd is the son of former Blackburn and QPR defender Christopher, who played 171 top-flight matches for those two sides, as well as a further 12 in the Championship with Aston Villa.The City forward is the younger of two brothers at the club, with Tyrone also involved in the youth team, and will now be aiming to play more first-team minutes after an exciting debut.As a fleet-footed forward, Floyd could not be more of a different player to his dad Christopher, who was a no-nonsense towering centre-back."Coming from under-21s to first-team training, that is a big jump," added Samba. "The sessions are more tiring, you have to run more - they demand more of you and you have to cope with it."Former Norwich striker Chris Sutton added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "Absolutely brilliant moment for Floyd. His dad was in the stadium and will be extremely proud. It's the journey, he has been nurtured at Man City, got his moment and what a night for him."He has given Enzo Maresca a bit of food for thought moving forward. Of course, he is not going to play ahead of Erling Haaland but it is a great evening for him and good for his development."Maresca can think he can trust him a little bit more."

schema.headline: Man City 5-0 Norwich: Floyd Samba debut overshadows JJ Gabriel saga

title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
description: Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.In a c
body: Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book, after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough." A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

schema.headline: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims

title: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief Rutte
description: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.The alliance'
body: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.The alliance's secretary general told the BBC he was "absolutely confident" in the UK's commitment to hit a Nato-wide spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.Speaking after meetings in London, he said British ministers accepted the need to make yearly steps towards hitting the target.But he accepted that the exact "pathway" towards the goal would not be set out until next year.Andy Burnham has followed predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in committing to reach Nato's 3.5% spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.He has said date for reaching a planned 3% interim target will come next spring, when the long-term budgets of government departments are due to be set.But he has faced pressure to immediately commit to reaching the milestone by the end of the decade. His chancellor and ex-defence secretary John Healey has previously argued this would show Britain was serious about the Nato goal.Former Dutch PM Rutte has been encouraging members of the alliance not to pencil in large spending increases shortly before the deadline.Speaking to BBC political editor Chris Mason after meeting Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Rutte said he was confident British ministers understood the 2035 target could not be met "in one go in 2034"."I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the 3.5[%] they are there," he said."I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there."There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year," he added.Rutte also said that defence spending should be separated out from the issue of welfare, adding that economic growth was the key to ensuring military commitments could be met alongside spending in other areas. The Conservatives have been pushing for hikes in defence spending to be funded through cuts to benefits, and have criticised Burnham for saying last week that national security "can't come at the expense of social security".Rutte added: "I don't know all the details of the UK economy, I think this is something this government is now navigating," he added. "But I would say these are two separate issues.""One is, indeed, spending on defence, but the other is of course making sure that the economy is growing enough, so you can distribute the success of a growing economy amongst various income groups, various issues in the Budget, for example welfare and healthcare and the pensions.""You have to do it all, and if you want to do it successfully, you need economic growth," he added. "Of course there are issues. I've been prime minister myself for 14 years. You have to take tough decisions, and it's not always easy." Elsewhere in his interview, Rutte said recent Russian military activity in western Ukraine which saw Poland close two of its airports on Thursday showed Vladimir Putin was "increasingly desperate" over his prospects for the war.Asked about the possibility of a Russian attack that could demand a Nato response, he replied: "If you are willing to sacrifice 1.2 million of your own people in this crazy unprovoked fight, let's not be naïve about what Putin could do."He also said there would be discussions among Nato allies over how to respond to the situation in the Red Sea, where Iran-aligned Houthis recently seized control of parts of Yemen's coast along the important shipping route.Saudi Arabia has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz."I would not be surprised if some phone calls were taking place between European allies, 'hey, how are we going to deal with this?'" he added."Let's see what happens, and if Nato can help, we will always be helpful".

schema.headline: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief Rutte

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton and Liam Dawson impress as hosts secure T20 series win in Cardiff
description: Second Vitality T20, CardiffSri Lanka 145-9 (20 overs): Nissanka 37 (21); Dawson 3-32England 146-4 (12.1 overs): Banton 52* (24); Rathnayake 1-25Engla
body: Second Vitality T20, CardiffSri Lanka 145-9 (20 overs): Nissanka 37 (21); Dawson 3-32England 146-4 (12.1 overs): Banton 52* (24); Rathnayake 1-25England won by six wickets; lead series 2-0ScorecardEngland's impressive T20 form continued as they thrashed Sri Lanka by six wickets in Cardiff to seal the series with a match to spare. Tom Banton's unbeaten 52 ensured England made light work of chasing a below-par 146, reaching the target in just 12.1 overs. Jos Buttler and Aneurin Donald raced to an opening stand of 51 in 4.3 overs before they both fell in the space of four balls for 30 and 21 respectively, but England's middle order followed suit in their aggression.Captain Harry Brook needed to score 49 to break Tilak Varma's record of 336 T20 international runs without being dismissed, and he looked on course, whacking three sixes in his 23 off just eight balls, before he was brilliantly caught by a diving Eshan Malinga.Banton then took on the charge, clubbing four sixes in his 24-ball knock as England remain unbeaten in the shortest format this summer.Brendon McCullum's side have now won 22 of their past 25 completed T20s since the start of last summer - a win percentage of 88%, with India (73%) the next best among full-member nations.England's fluency juxtaposed Sri Lanka's innings as the tourist batters struggled again, limping to 145-9 after being bowled out for just 135 in the opener on Tuesday.There will be added frustration from this innings, though, as their openers started so brightly by reaching 55-0 from the first five overs. But Liam Dawson took two wickets in the final over of the powerplay to halt their momentum and the middle order failed to recover, losing 9-90 thereafter and adding just 12 from a dire final four overs. Dawson finished with 3-32 and Jamie Overton 2-23, while Sonny Baker impressed again with his pace and control in a miserly spell of 1-15, including a wicket maiden in the 19th over.The series concludes at Old Trafford on Saturday and is followed by three one-day internationals.Though it is proving to be a mismatched series so far, England are building a well-balanced line-up under Brook's leadership and have barely broken sweat in notching a 2-0 lead.Sri Lanka's explosive start, led by Pathum Nissanka, who top-scored with 37, was the only time England have been on the back foot, but it was the ever-reliable Dawson who dragged it back, having become a mainstay in Brook's T20 line-up. The two soft dismissals highlighted Sri Lanka's woes - Lahiru Udara was caught at mid-on and Kamil Mishara chipped one straight back to the slow left-arm spinner. What followed was a series of soft dismissals, most caught trying to find the boundary, as Overton and Baker hammered away at a good length before Archer, who had started expensively, claimed two wickets at the death to revive his own figures.Sri Lanka managed just two sixes in their innings compared to England's 10, with it being only the seventh time their top five have all hit at least one in T20 internationals.Newcomer Donald started the carnage, ramping Dushmantha Chameera's first ball over the ropes, before Buttler joined the party and Brook then launched three of his own into the stands.England's intent was clear from the fact Donald's strike-rate of 161.54 was the lowest of the top five. Spinner Wanindu Hasaranga took most of the damage as he conceded 42 off just three overs, with a couple disappearing out of the ground.Banton, one of few batters to miss out in England's 254-4 on Tuesday, made the most of his opportunity to produce a fine finish by sweeping and striking firmly down the ground.England have set themselves up nicely to finish unbeaten in T20s this summer after thrashing India 4-0 earlier in the year.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton and Liam Dawson impress as hosts secure T20 series win in Cardiff

title: Human remains identified as mum missing since 2019
description: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandUpdated 7 hours agoHuman remai
body: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was last seen in December 2019ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandUpdated 7 hours agoHuman remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019. Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as  "long and complex". Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The human remains were found after a wildfire in south-west LondonPolice said they had followed more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, taken more than 300 statements and carried out detailed searches at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels.Det Ch Insp Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: "While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne's family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty."Throughout this investigation, Joanne's family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time."As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable."He stressed that the police would still like to hear from anyone with information about Sheen's disappearance.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the publicLondon Fire Brigade was called on 5 August to a blaze that damaged about two hectares of shrubland in an area known as Bedfont Pits. The human remains were discovered a week later, and a post-mortem examination suggested they had come from a woman aged between 25 and 45. A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed the remains were found by a member of the public at the site close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park.Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate a £20,000 reward for information that supports the investigation.Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 - two months after she was last seen.Several people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no charges were brought and the investigation remained unsolved.Police previously said she did not have a permanent place of address, a vehicle or a bank account.

schema.headline: Human remains identified as mum missing since 2019

title: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
description: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMo
body: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMoscow and DmitrovThe system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say."We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?Far from it.For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veteransAs for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.I said no surprises. But there have been some."Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns."The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:"The Communist Party, onwards we go!"We're with the people, don't you know?"More X Factor than exit poll.Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament."In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing. But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.And if a party doesn't support the war?One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election."The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me. "This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place."It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popularFor now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat."Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.The war is front and centre of people's minds here.Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation""We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen.""I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing."What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."Expectations are low that this election will change much."Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied."Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

schema.headline: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter

title: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes
description: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's dea
body: "Civilians in Iran are caught between gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed by their own government and the nation's deadly conflict with the United States and Israel," the fact-finding mission warned in a statement on Thursday.For their latest report to the UN Human Rights Council, the mission's three independent experts investigated two of the deadliest attacks on civilians during the conflict.On 28 February, when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Tomahawk missiles struck Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the southern town of Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities.The fact-finding mission's experts said the school was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) naval complex also attacked that day, but that the school was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated that it was used for military purposes.The experts said that, based on the evidence gathered - including media reports indicating that a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles - they had reasonable grounds to believe that the strike on the school was carried out by the US.They also concluded that the school was "the intended point of impact and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage" from the attack on the IRGC complex, citing survivors as saying the school was struck twice.The US military has yet to release the findings of its investigation into the Minab strike, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said it would "never target civilian targets".Also on 28 February, Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM) dispersed clouds of tungsten pellets over a sports complex and residential area in the town of Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to local authorities.Again, the fact-finding mission's experts said the sports complex was clearly identifiable and that no information indicated it was used for military purposes.They concluded by saying there were reasonable grounds to believe that the strike was carried out by the US, citing evidence including the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses PrSM missiles.The US military has said it carried no strikes on Lamerd that day and disputed reports identifying the weapon used as a PrSM.In both incidents, the fact-finding mission's experts said there were "reasonable grounds to believe that the US committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects".The fact-finding mission's report also covers the Iranian authorities' violent repression of the mass protests that took place across Iran in December 2025 and January 2026.The experts said it was an unprecedented escalation from past crackdowns, marked by the widespread use of lethal force resulting in mass killings and injuries, and extensive arrests.They cited witnesses, health workers and victims' families as saying that security personnel positioned themselves on rooftops and other elevated positions, firing their assault rifles into crowds.Protesters also sustained severe wounds to the head, chest and eyes from metal shotgun pellets, causing permanent blindness.As the crackdown escalated, security forces attacked healthcare facilities, beating and arresting wounded demonstrators and arresting some healthcare workers, which deterred victims from seeking life-saving care, according to the experts.They also found that the tens of thousands of people detained during the protests faced torture, solitary confinement and denial of legal counsel.The experts warned that the government had since intensified its use of the death penalty against protesters, with at least 29 men executed following expedited trials on charges connected to the unrest.The fact-finding mission's report noted that it was not possible to independently verify the death toll from the crackdown, but said there were strong grounds to believe that it was significantly higher than the official figure of 3,000, the majority of whom the government identified as members of the security forces or bystanders.The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) has said it has confirmed the killing of more than 7,000 people, almost all of them protesters.The fact-finding mission's experts concluded that Iranian authorities had committed "many gross human rights violations" during the crackdown, and that these amounted to "the crimes against humanity of murder, imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, and other inhumane acts, committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against a civilian population".Iranian authorities accused the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest and blamed the deaths on what they described as "terrorists" and "rioters".

schema.headline: UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes

title: Father of Noah Woods pays tribute to 'sweetest little boy'
description: People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.Helicopters, dog u
body: People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation."You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it"."The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."He finished the post by addressing his son."It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches"."It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond."I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

schema.headline: Father of Noah Woods pays tribute to 'sweetest little boy'

title: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
description: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.Each year more than 600 of t
body: The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton."We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern."Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue."Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said."I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language."Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting."It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games."Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.So what about the crocodiles?They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times."The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says."Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy."The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDearbail JordanBusiness reporter and Kevin PeacheyCost of living correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoThe Bank of England has h
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDearbail JordanBusiness reporter and Kevin PeacheyCost of living correspondentUpdated 8 hours agoThe Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August.On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.Other major central banks have increased rates to counteract higher prices. On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve announced its first hike in three years while the European Central Bank has raised rates twice since June.Of the nine members on the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), six voted to hold rates at 3.75% while three -  including the Bank's chief economist Huw Pill - wanted to raise them to 4%.While financial markets have priced in the possibility of several rate rises next year, Bailey said the global backdrop remained "hugely unpredictable at the moment".He said that for interest rates to come down there would need to be "an end of conflict in the Middle East... and energy prices coming really back to where they were before this conflict began".There were some positive notes from the Bank of England.It said the UK economy had been "more resilient" than it had expected and raised its prediction for economic growth from 0.1% to 0.4% for the period between July and September.It also said that because the effect of higher energy costs had not yet spilled over into other areas of the economy, food price inflation was now predicted to be 4% by the end of the year, less than the Bank's previous forecast of 6-7%.Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages.The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.'Knock-on effect'Image source, Andy PargeterThe move will have a significant effect on borrowers like Andy Pargeter from Flintshire and his wife. They are coming off a five-year fixed rate mortgage of 1.19% in November. Earlier in the year they had hoped that interest rates might be falling at this point. However with rates held steady they now expect to pay around £300 more a month."We're in a fortunate position where we're able to accommodate that [increase]," he told BBC News. But he expects it will have "a knock-on effect in terms of how much we potentially save every month"."It's definitely been something… I have constantly been thinking about."Bond sales pausedAlongside the interest rate decision, the Bank also said it would halt its so-called "quantitative tightening" (QT) programme.It will pause its annual sale of government bonds – which are a kind of IOU that can be traded on the financial markets – and will instead sell off smaller chunks over eight years.The Bank bought £895bn of mainly government bonds during periods of economic turbulence such as the global financial crisis and the Covid pandemic to help keep the economy on an even keel. This was known as "quantitative easing". Since 2022, it has been offloading the bonds, including through sales. This has contributed to higher interest rates – or yields – on bonds, making it more expensive for the government to borrow money.The Bank said discussions to put in place a plan to reduce the current £488bn stockpile of bonds had started a year ago, implying the decision was not related to the recent rise in long term borrowing costs.The news that the Bank of England is overhauling its QT programme prompted an immediate reaction. The yield on 30-year UK government bonds fell from 5.86% on Thursday morning to 5.75% following the Bank's announcement. Yields on 10-year bonds dropped from 5.31% to 5.22%.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues in this story? title: Man, 29, jailed for raping two 14-year-old girls in Bolton
description: A man has been jailed for 14 years for raping two teenage girls after encouraging them to drink alcohol at his flat.Sultani Bakatash, 29, an Afghan, m
body: A man has been jailed for 14 years for raping two teenage girls after encouraging them to drink alcohol at his flat.Sultani Bakatash, 29, an Afghan, met one of the girls on Snapchat before inviting her and her friend to his home in Georgina Court, Bolton, Greater Manchester, on 6 December.Bolton Crown Court heard the 14-year-old girls drank vodka and Coke and became so intoxicated they were passing in and out of consciousness before Bakatash raped and sexually assaulted them.Following a four-week trial, he was convicted of two counts of rape, one of sexual assault and one of assault by penetration. The judge said his work with the British Army in Afghanistan might mean he was not deported.One of the girls managed to escape from the flat and knocked on a neighbour's door, the court heard.She said: "He's trying to rape my friend. She's locked in. He's raping her."The court heard Bakatash encouraged the girls to keep drinking while taking only a sip himself and complimenting them on their appearance.Charlotte Rimmer, prosecuting, said he had arranged to meet the girls, encouraged them to drink and then seized the opportunity to rape them.She described him as "a man, intent on sexual gratification, regardless of what they wanted".The court heard both girls became so drunk they passed out and each witnessed the other being raped and sexually assaulted.The court heard one of the girls had suffered severe psychological harm, while the effects of the sexual assault on the other would stay with her for life.A probation report said Bakatash did not acknowledge his offending and assessed him as posing a continued high risk to women and girls.Bakatash fled the property after the offences and was arrested two days later at his brother's house.The court heard he had been in the UK for two years and had indefinite leave to remain, with his mother, two brothers and two sisters also lived in the country.Umar Shehzad, defending, said Bakatash had been shot and injured while working with the British Army in Afghanistan.He said Bakatash had left Afghanistan out of fear following the Taliban takeover in 2021 and had felt "overwhelmed" by living in a foreign country.The judge said Bakatash could be deported after serving two-thirds of his sentence, but added this might not happen because he had worked with the British Army and fled Afghanistan in fear following the Taliban takeover.

title: 'Putney pusher' investigation ongoing after suspect's death, police say
description: The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview"."They searched his home, and the Met Police press te
body: The family said that police "chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview"."They searched his home, and the Met Police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting," they said. "For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence."He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation, and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation."They said the police were repeatedly asked to end their investigation and warned about the impact it was having on Brandram's mental health, adding: "Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead."Brandram was linked to the incident in April when a person contacted officers with information that opened new lines of inquiry, according to the Met. His arrest was deemed proportionate by officers in order to seize and search his devices as part of the investigation. The force emphasised that it had not named Brandram publicly when he was arrested or at any point before his death. While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.Ch Supt Dan Knowles said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram's family and friends at this deeply distressing time. "We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him."He said that following Brandram's release under investigation, "it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations"."This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing," he added.Knowles, who leads policing in south-west London, said that cases involving "complex evidential and forensic work" could take "a number of months to complete". The Independent Office of Police Conduct confirmed it had received the Met's referral, which is being assessed.Shortly after the Putney Bridge incident on 5 May 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head."It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me."The Met said at the time that about 15 minutes after the push, the jogger came back the other way across the bridge and ignored the victim when she tried to speak to him.Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident.The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Balaclava boys on electric bikes: How to tackle the problem?
description: Image caption, A member of the public posted this image of young men in the Pentland Hills after witnessing a horse being spooked ByCalum WatsonBBC Sc
body: Image caption, A member of the public posted this image of young men in the Pentland Hills after witnessing a horse being spooked ByCalum WatsonBBC ScotlandUpdated 17 September 2026 06:04 BSTFrom the Pentland Hills near Edinburgh to the streets of the country's biggest cities, a common menace is causing irritation, alarm and in some cases even death.The sight of young men, their identities hidden by black balaclavas, tearing around on electric bikes or scooters is becoming a familiar one.The picture above was taken by a man who posted on social media about "morons on electric bikes" scaring a nearby horse, external as they rode illegally on public footpaths.Aside from being showered with gravel churned up by the "gobby" miscreants, no-one came to harm that day, but others have not been so lucky. Figure caption, Warning: Contains distressing scenes. Dashcam footage shows the aftermath of the crash that killed a pedestrian in SunderlandEarlier this year, a court was shown distressing dashcam footage of the moment a masked 18-year-old on an electric motorbike ploughed into a woman on a pedestrian crossing in Sunderland. Gloria Stephenson, 86, died at the scene. The rider - Billy Stokoe, who had taken cannabis and was using his mobile at the time of the crash - was jailed for more than six years for causing death by dangerous driving. Few would dispute that illegal e-bikes and scooters are a growing problem, but what can be done about it? Here are some of the options.Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues with electric bikes and scooters?Seize and destroy illegal bikesThe term e-bike is often used loosely to cover a range of different vehicles. Strictly speaking it refers to an electrically assisted pedal cycle (an EAPC) where an electric motor kicks in to take the strain off the rider while pedalling. By law, the motor cuts out at 15.5mph (25km/h) and its continuous power is capped at 250 watts.But these safeguards are easily bypassed by "tuning kits" or software hacks that make them capable of running much faster, sometimes in excess of 40mph. A quick search of online marketplaces reveals all sorts of modifications on offer, often shipped from eastern Europe, including motorbike-style twist grip throttles which allow the rider to accelerate without pedalling. Image caption, Modifications for e-bikes are openly advertised on online marketplacesThen there are electric dirt bikes from manufacturers such as Sur-Ron which look like mountain bikes but are capable of about 50mph - and 70mph or more if modified.  Unlike legal e-bikes they require a licence and insurance to be used in public spaces or on roads. E-scooters are also popular - despite it currently being illegal to ride them on public roads or pavements except in certain rental zones.What they all have in common is that they are expensive, ranging from a few hundred to several thousands of pounds, and modifications can cost hundreds of pounds more on top.Seizing and destroying them represents a significant penalty. A new law and rules introduced this summer gave police in England and Wales greater powers to seize illegal vehicles without the need for a formal warning if they are being used in an anti-social manner.In Scotland, ministers say they are in favour of increasing police seizure powers, although they point out bikes can already be seized under certain circumstances.Dedicated police teamsCatching the offenders is a problem for the police - it's a crime where its very nature means the suspects have a fast and highly manoeuvrable method of escape. A patrol car can easily be evaded by heading down a narrow alleyway or through bollards. David Kennedy from the Scottish Police Federation says more dangerous tactics are also employed. "These individuals on these bikes will come up one-way streets the wrong way so there's no way a police officer in a car or even on a motorbike would be safe to follow them," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast. Image source, Metropolitan PoliceImage caption, The Metropolitan Police say their fleet of electric dirt bikes is helping to cut crimeSome forces across the UK have responded to the challenge by setting up specialised units backed up by drones.In parts of inner city London, Metropolitan Police officers have been equipped with a fleet of 25 Sur-Ron dirt bikes - partly funded with proceeds of crime money. As part of a crackdown targeting mobile phone thefts - which in London often involve such bikes - they claim it has helped cut offences by 13,000 in a year. Figure caption, Gwent Police, in south Wales, have made use of drones to target illegal e-bikesA number of forces have successfully used drones to track illegal e-bike riders rather than engaging in risky pursuits.Officers monitor suspects from above, then their colleagues are directed to move in on foot to make seizures and arrests. In Devon and Cornwall officers have also sprayed illegal riders and their bikes with SmartWater - a forensic marking product that contains a unique chemical code which becomes visible using ultraviolet light. Action on face coveringsOne of the most sinister aspects of e-bike misuse is that riders often wear black balaclavas or "ballys".Whether it is a practical attempt to hide their identity or part of a youth sub-culture,  there is no doubt that many people find the sight of masked youths intimidating. The debate about the appropriateness of wearing balaclavas in public places goes wider than e-bikes, encompassing anti-social behaviour, crime and some anti-immigration protests.Image source, Danni MacRaeImage caption, A group of boys pictured on top of a former Debenhams store in Nottingham is an example of behaviour that has prompted the restrictions on face coverings New restrictions introduced just this week under Operation Reclaim in Nottingham give police and council officers the power to order people to remove face coverings, backed up by £70 fixed penalty notices. Exemptions apply for religious, medical and certain other legitimate reasons.David Kennedy from the Scottish Police Federation says there is definitely "more to do" on face coverings although he cautions that localised enforcement might simply see youths moving elsewhere. "If you are on an e-bike and you are wearing a face covering, the concern I have got is you are not wearing a helmet," he adds."I don't see many people travelling about the city centre on e-bikes wearing helmets."Target the parents or sellersMany parents are unaware that knowingly allowing their child to use an illegal e-bike or an e-scooter in a public place could land them with a fine or points on their driving licence.Under the current law, e-scooters can only be used legally on private land. The only exceptions are a number of rental trial zones,, external all of them located in England, yet some parents regard e-scooters as legitimate toys. Riders of legal electrically assisted pedal bikes must be at least 14, and any illegal modification means the bikes qualify as a motor vehicle/moped, requiring registration, a driving licence, tax and insurance. If an under-18-year-old is stopped by the police, their parents could potentially be accused of "causing or permitting" a driving offence with a possible £300 fine and six penalty points. And even a child too young to drive can have points added to a "ghost licence" which can transfer to their provisional when they are old enough to apply for one.Image source, Fubar NewsImage caption, Parents of children using e-scooters on a road or pavement could potentially face a fine and points on their driving licenceSome argue the problem needs to be addressed earlier, before a young person gets hold of an e-bike or e-scooter, by targeting the point of sale. This could range from clearer warnings about the rules, to a mandatory buyer information and registration scheme which would make it easier for police to trace vehicles used in crime or anti-social behaviour.Last year an all-party Westminster inquiry, external called for action to close a legal loophole that allows illegal vehicles to be sold under the guise of off-road use.The MPs also suggested that online marketplaces be held accountable for unsafe products such as the modification kits that are sold on their platforms. Offer young people something better to doMoral outrage at the behaviour of young people is nothing new and predates the invention of e-bikes by a considerable margin. Historians have found texts bemoaning declining standards dating back 4,000 years to ancient Mesopotamia. Some might argue the e-bike scourge is just the latest manifestation of an age-old problem and that rather than demonising the "bally boys" a better approach is to try to understand the boredom and frustrations that underpin the trend. In Aberdeen, alongside police enforcement action, one go karting centre is offering free sessions where e-scooter and e-bike riders can use them in a legal and safer environment.Figure caption, The push to make e-bike riding saferBut given the scale of e-bike misuse, can such schemes make an impact? The backdrop is a long-term decline in services for young people and financial pressures on local authorities and charities that provide them.A report from the YMCA, external last year found council-funded youth services in England and Wales have lost more than £1bn since 2010 with hundreds of youth clubs shutting and youth worker posts disappearing. Youth Scotland, citing research by Unison,, external paints a similar picture. Whether the answer is drones, dedicated police units or creating more positive ways in which young people can fill their day, the common denominator is fresh thinking and - arguably  the biggest challenge - extra resources.

schema.headline: Balaclava boys on electric bikes: How to tackle the problem?
